tracks.narration: Adding two bits is easy — but a carry can spread through every column. How does it actually move?
A half adder takes two bits A and B and produces a sum bit, X O R, and a carry bit, A N D. Good for one column, but it can't accept an incoming carry from the column below.
Stack two half adders. The first takes A and B; the second adds C in to that partial sum. An O R gate merges the two carry signals into C out.

Set A and B to one, and C in to one. The first X O R fires, then the second X O R fires, and finally the O R gate raises C out. Sum lands at one, C out lands at one — one plus one plus one equals binary one one.
Chain four of them and you add two four-bit numbers. The carry from each column has to settle before the next column can finish — that's why the rightmost adder fires first, then the next, and so on.
Each column is local. The carry chain is global — and that is what makes ripple-carry addition slow for wide numbers.
